items.title: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s
items.summary:
Porridge emerges as trend’s poster child with consumers looking to foods that help them feel full for longer, says Waitrose

Sales of filling foods such as porridge oats that mimic the effect of taking weight-loss medication are booming on the back of social media hype billing them as “nature’s Ozempic” or “oatzempic”.

Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s

items.title: In Waves review – love, grief and surfing at heart of profoundly moving animated tale
items.summary:
Tenderly drawn story combines a history of surfing with an emotional account of losing a partner to bone cancer aged 24

This gently moving and beautifully animated drama is adapted from an award-winning graphic novel by Californian illustrator AJ Dungo. His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe.

AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them.

Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the…
items.t: In Waves review – love, grief and surfing at heart of profoundly moving animated tale

items.title: Middle-aged women in England least likely to successfully quit smoking, study finds
items.summary:
Of nearly 8,000 women who tried to stop, only 18% of those aged 45 to 60 managed to give up

Middle-aged women in England are the least likely to successfully give up smoking, according to research.

Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and illness in the UK. While overall smoking rates in England have declined in recent decades, rates in some regions have increased. About 6.75 million people smoke in England, of whom around 14% are women aged 45-60.

Continue reading...
items.t: Middle-aged women in England least likely to successfully quit smoking, study finds

items.title: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds
items.summary:
People from lowest socioeconomic group in all countries studied had higher frailty scores than those in highest socioeconomic group

England has the largest gap between higher and lower socioeconomic groups when it comes to frailty compared with 30 other countries, a major study has found.

The research, led by academics at King’s College London and published in BMC Medicine, looked at levels of frailty in 71,703 people from 31 countries including England, the US, China, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia and Lithuania.

Continue reading...
items.t: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.
items.t: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

items.title: Thousands of immigrants with legal status lose Medicaid coverage
items.summary: Hundreds of thousands of immigrants living legally in the U.S. recently lost their Medicaid coverage under a provision of President Trump's signature tax and spending law. The law is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $900 billion over the next decade. Deema Zein reports on what that loss of coverage means for some of those affected.
items.t: Thousands of immigrants with legal status lose Medicaid coverage

items.title: ‘Not about notches on bedpost’: people in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults
items.summary:
Lancet survey shows under-45s have sex twice a month – down from four times in 1990 – and one in three under-25s have never had intercourse

Sex among British adults has slumped in recent decades, with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse.

The fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, or Natsal, found the average adult under 45 now has sex twice a month, continuing a downward trend from four times a month in 1990 and three times a month in 2010.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Not about notches on bedpost’: people in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults

items.title: This group of seamstresses mends shirts to make chemo easier for cancer patients
items.summary: Seamstresses in Ohio and other states are making zippered shirts for cancer patients so they can more comfortably undergo chemotherapy treatments.
items.t: This group of seamstresses mends shirts to make chemo easier for cancer patients

items.title: NHS trusts to be investigated over ‘repeated failures’ to admit treatment errors
items.summary:
Failing in their legal duty of candour adds to the distress of patients and families and damages trust, says England’s public service ombudsman

Hospitals will be investigated for regularly breaching their legal duty to tell patients and their relatives when mistakes have happened.

The public service ombudsman for England is launching an investigation into “repeated failures” by NHS trusts to discharge their “duty of candour” to admit when treatment errors have led to patients dying or suffering harm.

Continue reading...
items.t: NHS trusts to be investigated over ‘repeated failures’ to admit treatment errors

items.title: Life expectancy in Cuba falls for first time since 1950 amid economic crisis
items.summary:
WHO chief says life expectancy has fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 in 2025, figures that predate US fuel blockade

Life expectancy has fallen for the first time in Cuba since 1950 as the island reels from a severe economic crisis, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday.

On a visit to Havana, WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said life expectancy had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025, the first decline since records began in 1950.

Continue reading...
items.t: Life expectancy in Cuba falls for first time since 1950 amid economic crisis

items.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
items.summary:
Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life

Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing.

Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.”

Continue reading...
items.t: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out

items.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
items.summary:
Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate

Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children.

Continue reading...
items.t: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases

items.title: Summer heat deaths in 2026 reached record high of 5,258 in England
items.summary:
Figure for May to September is far higher than previous peak of 2,985 since records began a decade ago

More than 5,200 deaths in England in 2026 were linked to summer heat, the highest provisional annual total since records began a decade ago, according to the UK Health Security Agency.

The government agency said 5,258 deaths were associated with extreme heat between May and September 2026.

items.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
items.summary: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.
items.t: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

items.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
items.summary: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.
items.t: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

items.title: Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
items.summary:
Doctors are fighting an uphill battle against disinformation about routine vitamin K shots given to newborns in the hospital. It helps prevent a rare but devastating bleeding disorder.

items.t: Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K

items.title: The human cost of the electric vehicle boom is at the center of a lawsuit in Congo
items.summary:
A landmark lawsuit in Congo sees 27 residents accuse a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine of poisoning their community and the government of failing to protect them.

(Image credit: Marie Ruwet)
items.t: Bleeding, birth defects: Congo residents sue over alleged mining pollution

items.title: Soaring popularity of pickleball linked to eye injuries and disease, doctors warn
items.summary:
Woman hit in eye developed glaucoma as a result, with other injuries including retinal tears

Doctors have issued a warning about eye injuries linked to the rapid rise in popularity of pickleball, after a woman in her early 50s who was hit in the eye during a game developed glaucoma.

She sustained a direct hit to her left eye while playing without protective eyewear. The woman reported immediate blurry vision, severe pain and extreme light sensitivity. After emergency treatment, she was discharged from hospital and her symptoms seemed to be resolving.

Continue reading...
items.t: Soaring popularity of pickleball linked to eye injuries and disease, doctors warn

items.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
items.summary: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.
items.t: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease

items.title: Trump told the Army to pause the detonation of 9,500 pounds of lead azide in Iowa. Here's what to know
items.summary: The U.S. Army's controlled detonation of 68 barrels of unstable lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday is expected to produce a plume of dust containing lead particles that could extend as far as 100 miles away, a plan that residents, lawmakers and environmental groups say was not communicated appropriately.
items.t: Trump told the Army to pause the detonation of 9,500 pounds of lead azide in Iowa. Here's what to know

items.summary:

items.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
items.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.
items.t: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.
items.t: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

items.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
items.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.
items.t: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

items.title: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
items.summary: Wellness influencers say mushroom supplements can help with your gut health, focus and immune system. Here is where research suggests there are some links.
items.t: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?

items.title: The truth about dying: hospice workers on what loved ones should know
items.summary:
Anna Gordon met hospice care workers across the UK, learning how dignity and choice help create meaningful moments for patients

Most people in the UK actively avoid conversations about death and dying. They can be visibly uncomfortable when you raise the subject. When people try to talk about it, it tends to be euphemistically.

This is a mistake, one that can stop you from making important choices for yourself or your loved ones. It can increase fear and misunderstanding about what death can look like, while open conversations can help to ease these feelings and bring a sense of calm, peace and, on occasion, even beauty to the event.

Jenna Heritage: ‘Everyone’s big fear is that they are going to die in pain’

Continue reading...
items.t: The truth about dying: hospice workers on what loved ones should know

items.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
items.summary: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.
items.t: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells

items.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
items.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.
items.t: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
items.summary: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
items.t: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging

items.title: Patients may miss out on NHS weight-loss jabs in England after GP funding withdrawn
items.summary:
Inquiry finds most integrated care boards have scrapped payments to GPs for prescribing and monitoring the drug

Patients who are eligible for potentially life-changing weight-loss injections on the NHS risk missing out after most integrated care boards (ICBs) in England withdrew funding for GP services, an investigation has found.

The inquiry, conducted by the GP magazine Pulse, found that 21 of 36 ICBs have scrapped payments to practices for prescribing and monitoring Mounjaro, also known as tirzepatide. A further nine never had a local enhanced service and only four still retain one.

Continue reading...
items.t: Patients may miss out on NHS weight-loss jabs in England after GP funding withdrawn

items.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
items.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.
items.t: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

items.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
items.summary: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.
items.t: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds

items.title: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts
items.summary:
Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally

Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.

Continue reading...
items.t: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts

items.summary: Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints.
items.t: French activists demand a tear gas suspension over reported menstrual changes

items.summary:
From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex, a new book of short stories written by kids who are part of the "Read Alex" literacy program in Johannesburg. In one Johannesburg township, a reading club is instilling a love of books in kids — and inspiring them to become authors.

items.title: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’
items.summary:
Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Continue reading...
items.t: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’

items.summary:

items.t: It's Medicare open enrollment time. Here's what you need to know

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
items.t: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.
items.t: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

items.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
items.t: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

items.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
items.summary: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.
items.t: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

items.title: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a common blood pressure drug can activate calorie-burning brown fat in mice, potentially opening a new path toward improving metabolic health. An analysis of more than 100,000 patients also revealed surprising links between brown fat and lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, anxiety, and depression.
items.t: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat

items.title: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
items.summary:
The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma – a blood cancer linked to the herbicide.

(Image credit: Justin Sullivan)
items.t: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions

items.title: A doctor's guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication
items.summary: Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.
items.t: A doctor's guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication

items.title: Virginia child dies in state’s first measles-associated death of 2026
items.summary:
Death adds to national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 ⁠on Friday, involving a child who tested positive for the infectious disease, the state’s health department said.

The department said the child was ⁠age four or younger. It did not disclose additional details, including the child’s vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.

Continue reading...

items.title: Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal
items.summary:
Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

Continue reading...
items.t: Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal

items.title: Philadelphia neonatologist Joanna Parga-Belinkie on keeping babies safe from measles
items.summary: Amid ongoing measles outbreaks, Philadelphia neonatologist Joanna Parga-Belinkie talks with NPR's Scott Simon about how she keeps infants too young for the vaccine safe.
items.t: Philadelphia neonatologist Joanna Parga-Belinkie on keeping babies safe from measles

items.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
items.summary: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.
items.t: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

items.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
items.summary: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.
items.t: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

items.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
items.summary: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.
items.t: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
